title: Max turns his sandcastle into stone (with bacteria)

beats.text: A wave is about to hit Max's sandcastle. His kids are inside it.
Let's rewind to his first try.
Max wants a two-metre castle for his kids. Sand is just tiny rocks, he says, and rocks stack.
It pours into a 34-degree cone. Dry grains have nothing pulling them together.
One percent water forms tiny bridges whose surface tension pulls grains together. It holds 45 degrees.
More water is better? Full pores merge the bridges, and the heavy mud slumps.
Back to one percent, packed hard: seventy thumps, like the lab test. Tighter grains, more bridges. It stands.
Then the tide comes in. The moat fills first, water creeps into every pore, and the castle melts.
So Max sprays in soil bacteria, Sporosarcina pasteurii, the same microbes engineers use to make biocement.
The next wave melts it anyway. Bacteria alone glue nothing: to grow cement crystals, they need urea and calcium.
Three days in a urea and calcium chloride bath, two days drying: calcite glues every grain like sandstone. It releases ammonium, so gloves on.
The wave hits. It stands. Scientists bio-cemented a full-size dune in an Oregon flume: 19 trials, 300 waves each. Would you build one?
